background.definition: Seborrheic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the skin that occurs primarily in areas with a heavy density of sebaceous glands such as the face, scalp, chest, and back.

list.listitem: Seborrheic dermatitis affects 1% to 3% of the general immunocompetent population, with males affected more than females. It is usually more common and more severe in the winter months.
Global prevalence is estimated at 4.4%.
It is frequent in adolescents and young adults; however, people older than 50 years have consistently higher prevalence estimates than the general population.
Seborrheic dermatitis and tinea capitis are common in early childhood, with one survey showing age- and sex-adjusted prevalence of 10% in boys and 9.5% in girls.
In patients diagnosed with HIV/AIDS, prevalence is estimated to be between 34% and 83%.
Incidence in African Americans is slightly higher than the general population at approximatly 6%.

Psychological distress and poor self-image may negatively impact one's lifestyle. The Dermatology Quality of Life Index assesses the impact on patient decisions regarding social engagement, clothes being worn, and particpating in leisure activities.
Exact etiology is unknown, but common hypotheses include the following:
Inflammatory reaction to Malassezia spp (eg, Malassezia furfur, Malassezia ovalis) in the skin. This organism is also called Pityrosporum and Pityrosporum ovale.
Abnormal immune response.
Increased sebum levels in the skin (with the condition most prevalent after puberty, when sebaceous glands are most active and distributed in areas where sebaceous gland activity is greatest).
Hormonal influences (eg, androgenic influence on the pilosebaceous unit).
Nutritional deficits.
Environmental factors (eg, increasingly common in winter).
Neurogenic factors (eg, stroke and parkinsonism).
Abnormal humoral and cellular immune response to Malassezia spp on the skin.
Response to Malassezia spp may be due to toxin production or lipase activity.

Consider a diagnosis of seborrheic dermatitis in patients presenting with intermittent pruritus, burning, erythematous patches, and greasy scales over the nasolabial folds, postauricular skin, central face, and anterior chest. C

Diagnostic tests are not routinely recommended; consider histology to differentiate seborrheic dermatitis from other disorders, looking for neutrophils in the scale crust at the margins of follicular ostia. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pruritic flexural patches and plaques; family history of atopy
Annular scaling lesions; hyphae on KOH cytologic examination
Well-demarcated plaques on elbows, knees, scalp; nail pitting, onycholysis

Generalized seborrheic dermatitis-like eruption, often with systemic signs and symptoms such as fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, lytic bone lesions, anemia, thrombocytopenia, +/- jaundice, mandibular hyperplasia, and gingival inflammation
Malar rash, other systemic signs of SLE
Fixed centrofacial erythema or rhinophyma ± scalp involvement

list.listitem: Seborrheic dermatitis is defined clinically by the appearance of greasy, flaky, erythematous patches most commonly on the scalp, nasolabial folds, ears, eyebrows, and anterior presternal chest. Variations in symptom presentation are common.

Medallion seborrheic dermatitis is one presentation of seborrheic dermatitis of the chest, which appears initially as small, reddish-brown follicular and perifollicular papules with greasy scales and subsequently evolves into patches that resemble the shape of a medallion.
Pityriasiform seborrheic dermatitis of the chest is a rare form that presents with generalized macules and patches resembling pityriasis rosea, which infrequently causes erythroderma.

Sudden, pronounced onset of seborrheic dermatitis in young, otherwise healthy patients should alert the provider to the possibility of acquired immunodeficiency, such as HIV/AIDS. Seborrheic dermatitis may be more severe in HIV/AIDS patients, often with involvement of the extremities.

In patients with darker skin phototypes, erythema may be difficult to appreciate but hypopigmented patches in typical areas may provide a clue. Similarly, in children of color, infantile seborrheic dermatitis may present with erythema and flaking, along with hypopigmentation.
Diagnostic tests are not routinely recommended since seborrheic dermatitis is a clinical diagnosis.
Histology may be utilized to differentiate seborrheic dermatitis from other disorders. Neutrophils are generally present in the scale crust at the margins of follicular ostia.
Seborrheic dermatitis has a characteristic spongiform appearance on histologic examination.
History and physical examination are usually sufficient to make the diagnosis.
Histopathologic examination may be utilized to differentiate seborrheic dermatitis from other similar conditions.

Effective topcial treatments for seborrheic dermatitis of the face and scalp in adolescents and adults include topical azoles, ciclopirox, corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and lithium salt treatment. A

There is much uncertainty regarding the effectiveness and safety of various treatments for infantile seborrheic dermatitis (including cradle cap) such as emollients or shampoos and brushing, topical antifungals, and topical corticosteroids. B
Drug therapy can be broadly classified as antiinflammatory, antifungal, and keratolytic.

A Cochrane review of 36 RCTs involving 2706 adolescents and adults patients concluded that topical corticosteroids are effective in the treatment of seborrheic dermatitis of the face and scalp. In the short-term (up to 4 weeks of treatment), mild (Class I and II) and strong (Class III and IV) topical corticosteroids appear similarly effective and safe, based on low-quality evidence from one RCT involving 117 patients. However, in the long-term (defined as treatment >4 weeks), mild steroids resulted in better total clearance than strong steroids (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.63-0.98).

In the short-term, topical steroids are as effective and safe as topical azoles for total clearance of seborrheic dermatitis (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.94-1.32), but may reduce erythema and scaling more than azoles, based on moderate-quality evidence from 8 RCTs involving 464 patients.

Topical corticosteroids such as fluocinolone or fluocinonide solution, betamethasone valerate lotion, or desonide cream may be applied daily or twice daily until symptoms improve. Subsequently, use sparingly; continued use can lead to skin atrophy and telangiectasias. Patients who need continued steroids or who have frequent flares should be tranistioned to other effective treatments due to side effects. On the scalp, consider fluocinolone acetonide 0.01% shampoo once daily as an alternative to steroid ointment or cream. For more severe cases, intermittent, short-term use of clobetasol 0.05% shampoo twice weekly may be considered.

Topical calcineurin inhibitor (TCI) may also be effective for seborrheic dermatitis of the face and scalp. Topical steroids and TCIs appear similarly effective for short-term total clearance (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.88-1.32), based on low-quality evidence from 2 RCTs involving 60 patients. Additionally, topical steroids and TCIs are similarly effective for all other efficacy outcomes evaluated in 5 RCTs involving 237 patients. However, short-term side effects were less in the steroid group (RR 0.22, 95% CI 0.05-0.89), based on 2 RCTs (n = 60).
In the long-term (>4 weeks), TCIs appear as safe and effective as topical azoles in reducing erythema and scaling, based on one RCT.

TCIs such as tacrolimus and pimecrolimus may be applied once to twice daily but are not recommended for prolonged, regular use. They should only be applied to affected areas. Adverse effects from TCIs, including burning and irritation, may limit their use. Moreover, the prohibitive cost of TCIs may be a barrier for many patients.

Specifically for severe facial disease tacrolimus 0.1% decreased relapses and increased time betweeb relapse compared to 1% ciclopiroxolamine with twice weekly application for 25 weeks in one RCT of 114 patients.

Roflumilast 0.3% foam once daily, a topical phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor, appears to be effective and safe for the short-term treatment (8 weeks) of adult seborrheic dermatitis compared to placebo, based on 2 industry-sponsored RCTs. Comparison to other known effective topical therapies is needed, along with studies of longer duration. The price of 1 can of foam (60g) of roflumilast on goodrx.com (7/14/25) is around $1,000.

Lithium salt treatment, another antiinflammatory agent, was better than placebo for total clearance of seborrheic dermatitis in one RCT involving 129 patients (RR 8.59, 95% CI 2.08-35.52); side effects were similar. Additionally, lithium salt treatment was more effective than topcial azole for short-term total clearance, based on low-quality evidence from one RCT involving 288 patients (RR 1.79, 95% CI 1.10-2.90).

A Cochrane review of 51 RCTs involving 9052 adolescent and adult patients evaluating topical antifungals for the treatment of face and scalp seborrheic dermatitis found topical ketoconazole and ciclopirox to be better than placebo, but only limited evidence that either topical treatments is better than other medications within the same class. Topical ketoconazole appears as effective as topical corticosteroids, but with less adverse events. Important measures, such as quality of life (QoL), methodologically stronger studies, and better reporting of outcomes are needed.
Ciclopirox 1% shampoo, applied twice weekly for 4 weeks, is effective and safe in the treatment of seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp.

Ketoconazole 2% cream applied once or twice daily may be effective in treating nonscalp seborrheic dermatitis. Ketoconazole 1% shampoo 3 times per week may also be effective. Use may be decreased to twice weekly or as needed once disease is under control. Ketoconazole shampoo can be used long-term with no concerns for loss of efficacy.

Selenium sulfide 2.5%, crude coal tar, or 1% to 2% zinc pyrithione shampoo daily may have antifungal properties that reduce the number of yeasts on the skin and lead to symptom improvement. Other authors consider these agents topical keratolytics as well (see below).

Oral itraconazole 200 mg daily may be an effective treatment and may prevent relapses. It is typically given for 7 days, then as pulse therapy subsequently. Oral ketoconazole has been used at a dose of 200 mg daily for 4 weeks. Oral fluconazole and terbinafine have also been studied. Oral antifungals may have more side effects and medication interactions than topcial therapies and should only be considered after topical options have been exhausted.
Topical salicylic acid or crude coal tar can be used daily or every other day until symptoms are under control. Subsequently, frequency may be reduced to 2 to 3 times per week or as needed.
Dense, diffuse scales may be treated with keratolytics before topical corticosteroids are applied.
Metronidazole 1% gel applied twice daily for 8 weeks may be effective in the treatment of seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp and chest. There have been mixed results using this treatment on the face.

Isotretinoin may be considered in refractory cases to suppress sebaceous gland activity. Treatment with 0.1 to 0.3 mg/kg/day may result in improvement in severe seborrhea after 4 weeks of therapy. Maintenance therapy may be necessary for several years thereafter. Adverse side effects of retinoids limit widespread use.
Low dose isotretinoin 10mg alternate days in a randomized comparative trial showed significantly reduced sebum production compared to using only topical treatments.
UV-A and UV-B light inhibit the growth of Malassezia spp and result in symptom improvement during summer months.
The combination of clobetasol propionate 0.05% shampoo alternating with 2% ketoconazole shampoo may be more effective than ketoconazole alone.
Tea tree oil (Melaleuca oil) is an essential oil from a shrub native to Australia that appears to be effective and well tolerated when used daily as a 5% shampoo.
Aloe vera, tree tea oil, and Quassia Amaria may be effective for reducing scaling, pruritis and erythema, and may lead to full remission.

Seborrheic blepharitis is one of several causes of chronic anterior blepharitis. Careful and meticulous eyelid hygiene is the primary treatment. A Cochrane review of interventions for chronic blepharitis found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of any of the evaluated treatments, including topical antibiotics, topical steroids, oral antibiotics, and lid hygiene.
Refer patient to dermatologist if diagnosis is uncertain or seborrhea is severe, generalized, and unresponsive to treatment.
In one study, seborrheic dermatitis was the causative factor in 2% of cases of erythroderma (generalized exfoliative dermatitis), which often requires inpatient management.
In cases of bacterial superinfection, topical or oral antibiotics such as erythromycin or clindamycin, may be used twice daily until symptoms have resolved.

Erythroderma must be managed in an inpatient setting because of the high risk of electrolyte abnormalities, temperature dysregulation, dehydration, secondary bacterial infection, and high-output heart failure.
Seborrheic dermatitis usually begins in the late teens to early adulthood and has a relapsing-remitting course throughout one's lifetime. C
Relapses are common even after successful short-term treatment. C
Seborrheic dermatitis usually begins in the late teens to early adulthood and has a relapsing-remitting course throughout one's lifetime.
Relapses are common even after successful short-term treatment.
Prognosis is usually excellent with adequate response to pharmacotherapy.
Infantile seborrheic dermatitis (ISD) may be linked to adult seborrheic dermatitis.
A familial tendency toward ISD, as well as increased tendency toward allergy, was noted at 10-year follow-up.
Seborrheic dermatitis in HIV/AIDS patients is usually more explosive, inflammatory, and severe than in healthy patients, thus resulting in persistent seborrheic dermatitis.
Patients can be followed as needed once appropriate and effective treatment has been initiated.
Good hygiene and frequent face washing has been suggested as a way to improve seborrheic dermatitis.

Patients can be advised to wash their hair several days a week, weekly, or as needed with an antifungal shampoo. Some patients fear that washing their hair too often will cause a dry scalp. Health providers can explain that the scaling and flaking may improve rather than worsen with more frequent hair washing.
UV light may also improve seborrheic dermatitis; however, caution patients about excessive sun exposure and sun damage.
Patients with CNS disorders such as Parkinson's disease tend to have a more severe and recalcitrant form of seborrheic dermatitis.
It has been suggested that in CNS disorders there is increased pooling of sebum secondary to immobility, which allows overgrowth of Malassea spp.

ISD usually appears at about age 6 months and spontaneously resolves by age 8 to 12 months. When present on the scalp, it is called "cradle cap." Seborrheic dermatitis in infants may involve axillary patches, lacks oozing and weeping, and may be nonpruritic.

Infants who develop generalized seborrheic dermatitis, diarrhea, and failure to thrive should be evaluated for immunodeficiencies, such as Leiner's disease, severe combined immunodeficiency, chronic granulomatous disease, Tuftsin deficiency, and complement C5 dysfunction.

Histiocytosis X (Letterer-Siwe disease) may be seen with a seborrheic dermatitis-like scalp eruption, often with systemic signs and symptoms suggestive of this diagnosis, such as those of diabetes insipidus.
Riboflavin, biotin, and pyridoxine deficiencies have been associated with seborrheic dermatitis-like eruptions in infants.

Based on a Cochrane review of 6 RCTs involving 310 children, there is much uncertainty regarding the effectiveness and safety of various treatments for infantile seborrheic dermatitis (including cradle cap) such as emollients or shampoos and brushing, topical antifungals, and topical corticosteroids.
A common scalp treatment involves using mineral or olive oil to loosen scales which are then gently rubbed with a cloth or soft hair brush. There are no FDA-approved shampoos in this age group.

Mild cases may respond to hydrocortisone ointment or lotion with a mild, nonmedicated shampoo (if scalp involvement). Moderate or severe cases may require use of fluorinated steroids. During treatment, be aware that absorption of medication is greater in children than in adults. Topical corticosteroids, even hydrocortisone, may have systemic side effects. Ketoconazole cream has been used safely for 1 to 2 weeks.
Borage oil has also been successful, most likely secondary to its effects on fatty acids in the skin.
